20260823_model

2026-08-23

Contents

  1. Hypotheses
  2. Model Structure
  3. Data Exploration
  4. Model run
  5. Validation and Verification

(1) Hypotheses

The aim of this study is to assess whether there is an interactive effect between the intrinsic variation within the agroforestry system and the landscape heterogeneity on crop yield. And if there is one, then how does it shape the crop yield.

Hence, follwoing hypotheses are posed: H1: If in-field heterogeneity is included in the regional yield model, then the model will perform better (lower AIC) than the model that does not include the in-field complexity term. H2: How does the interactive effect or the separate effect of those differ between fields included in this analysis and what affects the shift between those.

(2) Model Structure

In order to adress the named hypotheses the following model was designed. The model is built to assess the effects of surrounding landscape, intrinsic spatial variation and field characteristica of the field (as environmental, design and management specifics) on field’s agroforestry yield performance and follows the following srtucture:

yield_tha ~ landscape heterogeneity (swf) + intrinsic variaton + field design

(1.1) landscape heterogeneity the effect of landscape heterogeneity is assessed throught the availability of small woody features around the field as studies show that those have an effect on yields performance. as in Galpern et al 2020 the approach of functional predictor is implemented as it is still unclear at what distance does the surrounding landscape has the biggest effect on yield an this possibly depends on field special characteristica. Hence, borrowing from Galpern et al pethodology refund:pfr function is implemented to model this relation.

(1.2) intrisic variation fields intrinsic variation is represented by the distance at which the sample of the yield was taken, agroforestry research suggests that the yield in agroforestry system depends on the distance of the crops sample to the tree line. the effect is modeled by a smooth function as it is not linear ans is scalar.

(1.3) field characteristica field characteristica are specific for each field an hence act as bias correction. such are fields environmental conditions, soil t4exture, age of the agroforestry system and the trees within it.

(3) Data Exploration

Following the Zuur et al protocol from 2010 the following data exploration procedure wqas completed: - outlier screening - distribution/homogeneity of the response - zero-inflation - collinearity - relationships - independence of observations

Matrices for every group and subgroup

df <- read.csv("C:\\Users\\Elizaveta/OneDrive - Universität Bayreuth\\Dokumente\\MasterThesis\\MA_RProject\\data\\AnalysisData\\20260823_full.csv")
# ---- Numeric Variables  ----
num_vars <- c("prop_swf", 
              "l_contag", "l_np", "l_sidi", "l_shdi", "l_ai", "l_ed",
              "distance_to_tree_strip", 
              "temp_C_mean", "sun_MJ_m2_mean", "precip_mm_sum",
              "clay", "sand", "silt",
              "mean_slope", "min_slope", "max_slope" ,
              "prop_swf_within", "fert_N", "treeage", "AFage", "area")

# ---- Surrounding landscape heterogeneity: small woody features  ----
swf <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, distance, swf_year, prop_swf) |>
  unique() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = distance, values_from = prop_swf) |>
  arrange(id)

id_order <- swf$id
swf_mat    <- as.matrix(swf[, -c(1, 2)])
grid     <- as.numeric(colnames(swf_mat))


# ---- Surrounding landscape heterogeneity: landscape metrics ----
landscape_metrics <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, l_contag, l_np, l_sidi, l_shdi, l_ai, l_ed) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_lm <- landscape_metrics$id
lm_mat    <- as.matrix(landscape_metrics[, -c(1)])
lm_cols     <- as.character(colnames(lm_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_lm)

# ---- In-field spatial variation ----
intrinsic_variation <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, distance_to_tree_strip) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_iv <- intrinsic_variation$id
iv_mat    <- as.matrix(intrinsic_variation[, -c(1)])
iv_cols     <- as.character(colnames(iv_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_iv)

# ---- Environmental: climatic variables ----
climatic <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, precip_mm_sum, sun_MJ_m2_mean, temp_C_mean) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_c <- climatic$id
c_mat    <- as.matrix(climatic[, -c(1)])
c_cols     <- as.numeric(colnames(c_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_c)

# ---- Environmental: soil ----
# adjust clay/silt/sand column names to match your dataset
soil <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, clay, silt, sand) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_s <- soil$id
s_mat    <- as.matrix(soil[, -c(1)])
s_cols     <- as.character(colnames(s_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_s)

# ---- Environmental: elevation ----
elevation <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, mean_slope, min_slope, max_slope) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_el <- elevation$id
el_mat    <- as.matrix(elevation[, -c(1)])
el_cols     <- as.character(colnames(el_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_el)

# ---- Field design ----
field_design <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, prop_swf_within, fert_N, treeage, AFage, area) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

id_fd <- field_design$id
fd_mat    <- as.matrix(field_design[, -c(1)])
fd_cols     <- as.character(colnames(fd_mat))

stopifnot(id_order == id_fd)


# ---- Identifiers ----
identifiers <- df |>
  dplyr::select(id, field) |>
  unique() |>
  arrange(id)

Distribution of the response variable: yield tha

ggplot(df, aes(x = seq_along(yield_tha), y = yield_tha)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Observation",
    y = "Yield (t/ha)"
  )

ggplot(df, aes(x = seq_along(yield_tha), y = yield_tha, color = crop_unified)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Observation",
    y = "Yield (t/ha)"
  )

ggplot(df, aes(x = seq_along(yield_tha), y = yield_tha, color = distance_to_tree_strip)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Observation",
    y = "Yield (t/ha)"
  )

ggplot(df, aes(x = yield_tha)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = "white") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of yield_tha")

ggplot(df, aes(x = crop_unified, y = yield_tha)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "yield_tha by crop", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

It is clear that the maize has a completely different scale of yield within the dataset. It is because in comparision to all the other crops sillage maize is produced only to feed the animals and hence the whole biomass is harvested and not only the grain as it is for all the other crops. Hence, the yield is on a different scale and all teh yield in the dataset has to be scaled in order for the results to be interpretable and consistent across crops.

Interpretation

Variable Negative Cor Positive Cor Interpretation
prop_swf correlates negatively with contagion index l_contag (-0.41), slightly negative with clay (-0.21), slightly negatively with all field design parameters fert_N (-0.19), treeage (-0.18), AFage (-0.26), area (-0.34).
slightly positive cor with mean slope (0.20), with min slope (0.27), with proportion of swf within the field (0.36). CONTAG is an ‘Aggregation metric’. It is based on cell adjacencies and describes the probability of two random cells belonging to the same class. The more small woody features the less aggregated the landscape is, probably because swf introduce little patches disrupting the landscape. Clay: no interpretation. Slope: no interpretation (maybe trees enjoy it on slopes but that’s an uneducated guess). Field design: no interpretation. l_contag correlates negatively with min slope (-0.54), mean slope (-0.49), prop_swf (-0.41), l_shdi (-0.39), l_sidi (-0.53) edge density l_ed (-0.34), prop_swf_within (-0.22), sand (-0.20), precip_mm_sum (-0.19).
correlates strongly positively with area (0.74), treeage (0.52), AFage (0.50), aggregation index l_ai (0.34), clay (0.32). Landscape metrics were calculated within 3000m buffer including the field, meaning large fields build large class areas increasing the contagency index. Negative correlation with shannon and simpson due to the opposite nature of the metrics. l_np
negative correlation with l_ai (-0.75), with temp_C_mean (-0.56), sun radiation (-0.37), sand (-0.36), max slope (-0.31), fertilization (-0.30), treeage (-0.29)
positive correlation with l_shdi, l_ed (0.76), precipitation (0.49), clay (0.39), silt (0.32), mean slope (0.32), min slope (0.45) number of patches in the 3000m buffer. Wetter/cooler and flatter fields tend to have more landcover class patches. l_shdi correlates negatively with prop_swf_within (-0.59), treeage (-0.46), aggregation index l_ai (-0.41) and area (-0.41), l_contag (-0.39), temp_C_mean (-0.29), sand (-0.28), sun_MJ_m2_mean (-0.21).
correlates positively with mean slope (0.65), min slope (0.58), edge density l_ed (0.45), max slope (0.43), clay (0.32), precip_mm_sum (0.31), silt (0.22).
Shannon diversity index, i.e. how many land-cover classes are present and how evenly they are distributed. Steeper fields correlate with more diverse landscapes. Prop_swf_within gives negative correlation, the more swf in the field the lower the shannons index - might be because one class is prevaling in the field and hence reduces the shannons index, Treeage: no interpretation. Climate/soil correlations: no interpretation. l_sidi NA NA
no slight positive with AFage (0.22). uncorrelated with everything , so not confounded with any of the field-level landscape or environmental variables, good sign. temp_C_mean
correlates negatively with l_shdi (-0.59), AFage (-0.46), area (-0.42), l_ai (-0.41), max slope (-0.31), sun_MJ_m2_mean (-0.25), l_contag (-0.22), temp_C_mean (-0.18). correlates positively with prop_swf (0.36), l_ed (0.36), min slope (0.35), precip_mm_sum (0.32), mean slope (0.19). Most interesting is the correlation with AFage, as it implicates that older fields tend to have less small woody feateres on the field than younger ones. That might be confounded as sometimes trees are harvested, hence we see no correlation with treeage. fert_N
correlates positively with l_contag (0.50), clay (0.47), area (0.42), max slope (0.37), treeage (0.35), sun_MJ_m2_mean (0.34), l_ai (0.25), fert_N (0.25), distance_to_tree_strip (0.22). Negative correlation with aggregation is interesting, though no interpretation. Soil structure: I think those are mostly random as the AFage shpuld have no effect on soil structure. area correlates negatively with min slope (-0.82), l_ed (-0.65), mean slope (-0.63), precip_mm_sum (-0.55), prop_swf_within (-0.42), l_shdi (-0.41), prop_swf (-0.34).
correlates strongly positively with treeage (0.77), l_contag (0.74), l_ai (0.65), AFage (0.42), sun_MJ_m2_mean (0.29), temp_C_mean (0.23). confounded with field itself as only one value per field

Interpretation Summary

  • Landcover metrics correlated highly with all other metrics included in the dataset. Different metrics to different degrees, but still.
  • Area is a confounded metric as it seems continous and numeric, but it is bound directly to the field and does not differ from its name. It might have to be excluded as it is not an intrinsic para,eter it is the way the field is, and not the way it became due to some reasons.Also the graph below shows that we cannot see any relationship between area and yield.
  • Only l_ed or l_ai should be left in the model.
ggplot(df, aes(x = field, y = treeage, fill = area)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Tree age by field", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggplot(df, aes(x = field, y = yield_tha, fill = area)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Yield by field", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Relationships between yield and candidate predictors

df |>
  select(id, distance, prop_swf) |>
  distinct() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = distance, y = prop_swf)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "prop_swf as a function of distance from the field boundary")

my.yield <- df |>
  distinct(id, field, year, yield_tha, distance_to_tree_strip, crop_unified,
           fert_N, treeage) |>
  mutate(field = factor(field), crop_unified = factor(crop_unified), year = factor(year))

xyplot(yield_tha ~ distance_to_tree_strip | field, groups = crop_unified,
       data = my.yield, type = c("p", "r"), auto.key = TRUE)
